Record date: 2129-08-28
South Elizabeth Seychelles Hospital INTERNAL MEDICINE DEPARTMENT Location: 4923 Olivia Parkway Suite 217, Lake Jennabury
PATIENT: Lysander Fairfax Phone: 28451903 email:bradleymorgan@example.org DATE OF BIRTH: 1947-05-12 AGE: 80 years
FOLLOW-UP DATE: 08/28/29 FOLLOWED BY: Dr. Emily Carter
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Worsening shortness of breath, increased fatigue, and persistent lower extremity edema.
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Lysander Fairfax presents for follow-up after one week of treatment adjustments. He reports a deterioration in his shortness of breath, stating that he now experiences significant dyspnea even with minimal exertion. He notes that his productive cough has intensified, with increased yellow-green sputum production and a foul odor. He expresses concern over the persistent bilateral lower extremity edema, which has not improved despite the recent increase in diuretic therapy.
Mr. Fairfax mentions that he has had several episodes of nocturnal awakening due to breathlessness and has been relying on supplemental oxygen at home to maintain adequate oxygen saturation levels. He describes his overall energy levels as severely diminished, impacting his ability to perform activities of daily living.
REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General - + fatigue, - weight gain, + chills, - night sweats. Pulmonary - + worsening shortness of breath at rest, + increased productive cough with yellow-green sputum, - hemoptysis. Cardiac - no chest pain, + orthopnea, - paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Gastrointestinal - no nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Musculoskeletal - + joint pain, + persistent bilateral lower extremity edema. Neurological - no dizziness or headaches.
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: - Blood Pressure: 148/90 mmHg - Heart Rate: 92 bpm - Respiratory Rate: 26 breaths/min - Oxygen Saturation: 82% on room air, improved to 90% on supplemental oxygen.
General: The patient appears fatigued and in significant respiratory distress, utilizing accessory muscles for breathing.
HEENT: No nasal flaring, oropharynx clear.
Lungs: Diminished breath sounds bilaterally, with pronounced wheezing and bilateral crackles noted throughout.
Cardiac: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs or gallops.
Extremities: Severe bilateral lower extremity edema with pitting, extending to the thighs, with tenderness on palpation.
ASSESSMENT
1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbation, likely due to infection; sputum characteristics raise suspicion for possible bacterial infection. 2. Congestive heart failure with persistent fluid overload; current diuretic regimen appears inadequate. 3. Insomnia with significant impact on quality of life; ongoing pharmacological management requires further evaluation.
PLAN
1. Obtain a sputum culture and sensitivity to identify potential pathogens and guide antibiotic therapy. 2. Initiate systemic corticosteroids with a tapering dose of prednisone starting at 60 mg daily for 7 days to address acute exacerbation of COPD. 3. Increase furosemide to 480 mg daily and consider the addition of intravenous diuretics if no improvement in edema is noted; monitor renal function closely. 4. Continue nebulized albuterol every 2 hours and nebulized budesonide every 6 hours; add ipratropium bromide to optimize bronchodilation. 5. Consider hospitalization for further management of COPD exacerbation if symptoms do not improve with outpatient therapy; monitor closely for signs of respiratory failure. 6. Expedite the sleep study referral and consider adjusting insomnia management strategy; discuss the potential use of trazodone for sleep disturbances. 7. Educate Mr. Fairfax on recognizing signs of worsening respiratory distress and the importance of adherence to the treatment regimen.
Mr. Fairfax verbalized understanding of the treatment plan and the need for close monitoring of his symptoms.
DISPOSITION
Mr. Fairfax was advised to return for reevaluation in 3 days or sooner if his symptoms worsen. A follow-up appointment was scheduled for 09/02/29, with instructions to seek immediate medical attention for any acute exacerbations of respiratory distress, chest pain, or sudden weight gain.
